profile.name: Mervin Tabernero
profile.tagline: Transitioning from healthcare IT into SOC operations, focused on threat detection and Azure security.

alerts.whatTriggered: A process (PID 1864, masquerading as svchost.exe) opened a handle to lsass.exe (PID 840) and performed 1456 reads of process memory. This behavior is the exact definition of Defender's "Sensitive Credential Memory Detection (T1003.001 -LSASS Memory) is built to catch.
alerts.whyTriggered: The LSASS holds cached credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets in memory. Any non-system process reading its memory space is treated as high confidence credential-theft indicator, especially when accompanied by  a masquerading binary and a known credential-theft tool DLL loads.
alerts.whatHappened:
At 11:03:02 PM SOCSIM\dave.brown authenticated via a Network logon with domain Admin rights - the point at which the account was already compromised. At the same time, a svchost.exe process was spawned remotely via WMI, sourced from SOCSIM-SRV01 (172.31.6.185).
At 11:03:49 PM, a malicious file name svchost.exe was pushed to the DC via $$ administrative share (SMB) from 172.31.6.185 and  executed from C:\WIndows\Temp\ -- not the legitimate System32 location. It ran with the command line:
svchost.exe privilege::debug sekurlsa::logonpasswords exit
This is a well known Mimikatz CLi syntax: privilege:: debug elevates the the SeDebugPrivilege required to touch LSASS, and sekurlsa::logonpasswords is Mimikatz's core credential dumping module.
Immediately after the execution, the process loaded cryptdll.dll, samlib.dll, WinSCard.dll, and hid.dll in sequence -- the signature DLL -loading fingerprint of Mimikatz. It then opened a handle to the lsass.exe and, at 11:05:57 PM read its process memory (1456 reads/65402258 bytes copied).
Defender detected and quarantined the dropped file (EUS:Win32/CustomEnterpriseBlock) as a remediation -- but this remediation occured after the process had already executed  and begun reading LSASS memory (11:06:36PM), not before.
alerts.evidence:
[1864] svchost.exe  — Path: C:\Windows\Temp\svchost.exe (masquerade — real svchost = System32)
Command line: privilege::debug sekurlsa::logonpasswords exit
SHA1: e3b6ea8c46fa831cec6f235a5cf48b38a4ae8d69 (mimikatz.exe hash)
Integrity level: High | User: SOCSIM\dave.brown (real svchost = SYSTEM/System integrity)
Source device: SOCSIM-SRV01 / 172.31.6.185, delivered via C$ admin share
lsass.exe read: 1,456 reads, 6,402,256 bytes copied
Defender remediation: EUS:Win32/CustomEnterpriseBlock — quarantined post-execution
alerts.verdictJustification: Multiple indicators confirm malicious credential-theft activity: (1) a binary masquerading as a legitimate svchost.exe running from a non-standard location with elevated permission under a standard user account., (2) literal Mimikatz command line sysntax, (3) the signature Mimikatz DLL-loading pattern, (4) delivery via lateral movement over WMI/SMB admin shares from an internal host, (5) a Domain Admin account authenticating and conducting hands-on-keyboard activity, and (6) Defender's own correlation of the alert into a High-Severity, 19/23 aleet incident titled "Hands-on keyboard attack was launched from a compromised account".
investigationSteps: Opened the Alert "Sensitive credential memory read" in Defender and reviewed the alert story/Process Tree
Noted the affected host was a Domain COntroller (socsim-dc) and the account was SOCSIdave.brown -- classfied as high risk given the machine involved is a Domain controller.
Checked the linked incident('Hands-on keyboard attack was launched from a compromise account') to understand the broader attack chain rather than viewing the alert in isolation.
Walked the process tree chronologically: identified the 11:03:02:PM Domain Admin network logon and WMI-based remote process creation.
Pulled the raw process/event detaisl for PID 1864 and confirmed the path (C:\Windows\Temp\ - not system32), the command line, and the SHA1/creation time mismatch indicating a pre-staged tool.
Review the loaded - files( crypt.dll, samlib.dll, WinSCard.dll, hid.dll) abd recognized the Mimikatz DLL fingerprint.
Confirmed the handle-open, and memory-read events  against lsass.exe (PID840), noting the byte count and read count as evidence of a completed dump, not just an attempt.
Checked Defender's remediation status and confirmed the file was quarantined, but onluy after the credential-read activity already occured.
Mapped all the observed behavior to the MITRE ATT&CK techniques for the write-up
alerts.containment:
Force and immediate credential reset for SOCSIM\dave.brown and treat the account as fully compromised, not just the endpoint.
Isolate soc-sim and SOCSIM_SRV01 (172.31.6.185) pending full forensic review.
Audit all activities ferformed under dave.brown's Domain Admin sessions.
Revoew SOCSIM-SRV01 for how it was compromised.
Hunt across the environment for the same file hash (e3b6ea8c46fa831cec6f235a5cf48b38a4ae8d69) or the same cmdline pattern (sekurlsa::logonpasswords) on other hosts.
alerts.lessonsLearned:
Detection worked but the remediation happened only after Mimikatz had already loaded.
The path mismatch (Temp VS System32) was the single fastest tell that this was not a legitimate svchost.exe -- worth remembering to check process image path first.
Remember to chekc for a linked incident before writng up any individual alert.
This was a good first exposure to reading Mimikatz CLI syntax and associated DLLs -- worth commiting to memory as fast-recognition patterns for future alerts.

alerts.alertName: Credential Dumping via SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM Hive Export and LSASS Memory Access (LaZagne)
alerts.whatTriggered: Defender detected reg.exe exporting the SAM registry hive (HKLM\SAM) to a randomly named file in C:\Windows\Temp (nlurrk). The export was launched by svcmon.exe, an unsigned binary running from C:\Windows\Temp\svcmon\ that Defender associates with the LaZagne credential-recovery tool. The same process later opened lsass.exe for memory reading.
alerts.whyTriggered: The SAM hive stores local account names and NTLM password hashes. Windows locks the on-disk hive (C:\Windows\System32\config\SAM) while the OS is running, so attackers use the built-in reg.exe save command, which reads the hive through the registry API with admin/backup privileges and writes a copy that can be taken offline. reg.exe itself is a legitimate Windows binary; the detection is behavioural. Exporting the SAM hive (especially together with SYSTEM and SECURITY) to a temp folder is a high-fidelity credential-dumping pattern that rarely occurs in normal administration.
alerts.whatHappened:
A process running as SOCSIM\john.admin was launched through WMI (WmiPrvSE.exe --> cmd.exe) indicating remote or scripted  execution rather than an interactive user session. That cmd.exe (PID 4040) set the TEMP/TMP environment variables to C:\Windows\temp and executed svcmon.exe all redirecting all output to svcmon.log. The all argument is LaZagne's command-line syntax for running every credential-harvesting module (windows, browser, WiFi, admin tools and more) and the file hash was matched to LaZagne_latest.exe. The binary has been renamed to look like a benign service-monitoring tool.
Two svcmon.exe processes were observed (PIDs 6436 and 2668). This is consistent with LaZagne being packaged with PyInstaller, whose one-file executables start a bootloader process that launches a child copy of itself. 
LaZagne’s Windows module first ran cmd.exe /c ver to identify the OS version, then used reg.exe save to export three hives to randomly named files in C:\Windows\Temp: HKLM\SAM exported to C:\Windows\Temp\nlurrk, HKLM\SECURITY to C:\Windows\Temp\fyxwdjwbpf, and HKLM\SYSTEM\ejatqftik
Finally, svcmon.exe opened a handle to lsass.exe with PROCESS_VM_READ, PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION and PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION access rights and performed 312 memory reads totalling 39,380 bytes. This was a targeted read of LSASS memory, not a full process dump, consistent with a tool searching memory for credential material from logged-on sessions. Defender detected the activity but no automated remediation (process kill or file quarantine) was recorded.
alerts.evidence:
cmd.exe /c set TEMP=C:\Windows\Temp&&set TMP=C:\Windows\Temp&&C:\Windows\Temp\svcmon\svcmon.exe all > C:\Windows\Temp\svcmon\svcmon.log 2>&1
cmd.exe /c "ver"
cmd.exe /c "reg.exe save hklm\sam C:\Windows\Temp\nlurrk"
cmd.exe /c "reg.exe save hklm\security C:\Windows\Temp\fyxwdjwbpf" 
cmd.exe /c "reg.exe save hklm\system C:\Windows\Temp\ejatqftik"  
C:\Windows\Temp\svcmon\svcmon.exe (PIDs 6436 / 2668)
SHA-256: dc06d62ee95062e714f2566c95b8edaabfd387023b1bf98a09078b84007d5268
Parent chain: WmiPrvSE.exe → cmd.exe (PID 4040) → svcmon.exe → cmd.exe → reg.exe (PID 2412
LSASS access:Access mask: VM_READ + QUERY_INFORMATION + QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION; 312 reads / 39,380 bytes
alerts.verdictJustification:
1. Masquerading tool: svcmon.exe is not a Windows or known vendor binary; it runs from C:\Windows\Temp\svcmon\ and its hash matches LaZagne, a publicly available credential-dumping tool.
2. Remote execution chain: the activity began from WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd.exe under a privileged account, a common lateral-movement and remote-execution pattern, not normal interactive admin work.
3. Credential staging: SAM, SECURITY and SYSTEM were exported together to randomly named files in a temp folder. There is no legitimate administrative reason for this combination.
4. LSASS memory access: a non-security, non-system process read LSASS memory, which is how credentials of logged-on users are harvested.
alerts.queries:
1. Opened the alert in Microsoft Defender and reviewed the alert story and process tree.
2. Identified the affected asset as a server (SOCSIM-SRV02) and the account as SOCSIM\john.admin, a privileged account already classified as High risk.
3. Opened the linked incident (SOCSIM - INC 002 IRONWOOD) to view this alert in context with related alerts rather than in isolation.
4. Walked the process tree chronologically: WmiPrvSE.exe → cmd.exe (PID 4040) → svcmon.exe (PIDs 6436/2668) → cmd.exe → reg.exe, noting the WMI parent as a sign of remote execution.
5. Reviewed the command lines. The all argument and random temp filenames matched LaZagne’s known behaviour.
6. Checked the SHA-256 of svcmon.exe, which matched LaZagne_latest.exe, confirming the binary is renamed LaZagne.
7. Confirmed the three reg.exe save operations (SAM, SECURITY, SYSTEM) and their output paths.
8. Confirmed the LSASS process-access event, access rights requested, and the number and size of memory reads.
9. Checked the remediation status: the activity was detected but not blocked, and no automated remediation was taken.
10. Pivoted to Sentinel (queries below) to confirm file creation/deletion of the hive exports, look for outbound connections, and hunt for the hash on other hosts.
11. Mapped the observed behaviour to MITRE ATT&CK (Section 7).
alerts.containment:
1. Isolate SOCSIM-SRV02 in Defender to stop further credential use and lateral movement. Collect an investigation package first if possible.
2. Treat SOCSIM\john.admin as compromised: disable or reset the password, revoke active sessions, and review its sign-ins and activity from 03:34 onwards across all hosts.
3. Reset every credential exposed on this host: all local accounts (especially the local Administrator; if the same password is reused on other servers, reset those too), any service-account passwords stored as LSA secrets, and domain accounts with cached logons or active sessions on SOCSIM-SRV02.
4. Find the origin of the WMI execution: review logon events (4624 logon type 3) on SOCSIM-SRV02 around 03:34 to identify the source host, then investigate that host as the likely point of compromise.
5. Preserve and remove artefacts: collect svcmon.exe, svcmon.log and the three hive exports as evidence, then delete them from C:\Windows\Temp.
6. Hunt environment-wide for the SHA-256 hash, the svcmon.exe filename, and reg.exe save hklm\sam command lines (Query 4). Block the hash as a Defender custom indicator.
alerts.lessonsLearned:
1. Command-line arguments can identify a tool. The all argument pointed to LaZagne before the hash check confirmed it. Next time, I will research unusual arguments early.
2. A trusted binary can do untrusted things. reg.exe is legitimate, so the malicious signal came from its parent process, its arguments and its output location, not from the executable name.
3. SAM needs SYSTEM. Seeing all three hives exported together shows the attacker intended offline decryption, which increases confidence in the verdict and widens the scope of credential resets.
4. Record times with a timezone and consistent hash types. I will set the Defender portal to UTC and label hashes (SHA-1 vs SHA-256) so timelines and hunts are accurate.
5. Detection is not prevention. Check the remediation status of every alert. A high-confidence alert that was not blocked changes the urgency of escalation.
Go to Sentinel sooner. Confirming file deletion, outbound activity and hash prevalence with KQL turns "likely" into "confirmed."
